sentences.text: After the snow, a red mitten sat alone on a park bench.
It was small, woolly, and a little wet around the thumb.
A dog walker went by. A jogger went by. Nobody stopped.
At noon the park keeper noticed the bright red shape.
She shook off the snow and carried the mitten to the gate.
She placed it in the lost-and-found box and wrote a clear sign.
The sign said, Red mitten. Ask here.
Later, a neighbor spotted the sign and remembered the bench.
The neighbor took the mitten home in a dry bag.
A clear sign had helped a lost thing get back toward its street.

questions.prompt: What is this story mostly about?

choices.text: How a clear sign helps a lost mitten get picked up
How to knit a new pair of mittens
Why joggers race in deep snow
A bench that is moved to a new park

questions.explanation: People pass the mitten until the keeper makes a sign. Then a neighbor finds it. The sign is what changes the story.

questions.prompt: Where does the park keeper put the mitten?

choices.text: Inside a nest in a tree
In the lost-and-found box by the gate
On the highest hill in town
Under the snow on the bench

questions.explanation: The keeper carries the mitten to the gate and places it in the lost-and-found box. She does not leave it on the bench.

questions.prompt: Why is the mitten easier to return after noon?

choices.text: The snow melts the mitten into a puddle
The jogger hides it in a pocket
A sign tells people what was found and where to ask
The bench walks down to the gate

questions.explanation: Before noon, people walk past. After the keeper writes the sign, a neighbor knows what to do. The sign is the clue that makes the return possible.
